newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German metal workers ready for full strikes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German metal workers ready for full strikes.

text.p: German's largest trade union, IG Metall, warned on Tuesday that full strikes in the metal and engineering industries were now possible following the collapse of attempts to resolve a bitter row on planned cuts to sick pay.

Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the three-million-strong metal and engineering union, said the failure early on Tuesday of crisis talks in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia represented the last chance to solve the dispute "amicably".

He added that IG Metall's regional wage committees would be cancelling worker wage contracts early next year in a move that would allow them to conduct strikes from around March if no progress looked likely in the regular wage round for 1997.
Referring to the potential for strikes after the four-week notice period required under German law, Zwickel said in a statement: "If no peaceable settlement is reached, we shall indeed do that."

Employers across German industry have been complaining for years that high German wages and other employee costs have undermined their international competitiveness, and ultimately contributed to the country's near four-million jobless total.

The new law cutting worker sick pay to 80 percent from 100 percent has already triggered nationwide protests by metal and engineering workers. There have even been walkouts by staff in the usually much more peaceable banking and chemical sectors.
The law was introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government as part of an austerity package aimed at securing Germany's entry into European economic and monetary union.

IG Metall, in membership terms the largest union in the world, represents workers at key German industrial concerns including Daimler-Benz AG, electronics firm Siemens AG, and carmakers BMW and Volkswagen.
Zwickel accused employers of having wasted their best chance of solving the dispute on sick pay, which companies remain determined to reduce.
But negotiators for the employers' side said that a scheme to which IG Metall had been willing to agree under which sick pay costs would be offset by lower bonuses elsewhere, was simply not workable.
"We discussed this idea at length but concluded that it contained so many problems, incalculables and inequalities..." employers' negotiator Martin Kannegiesser told German radio.

Given the extent of feeling shown so far against the cuts, any industrial action could be far more extensive and damaging than last year's strike by Bavarian engineering workers or 1993 strikes by metal workers in east Germany.
The talks in North Rhine-Westphalia had been the latest of three high-profile efforts to resolve the dispute on wages and labour costs since the passing of the sick pay law.
But industrial relations in the sector slumped to an almost unprecedented low after a number of firms led by Daimler tried unsuccessfully to implement the new law without union consent.

Since then talks have focused on ways to secure the envisaged cost savings from the new law, estimated at up to 12 billion marks ($7.93 billion) across the whole of German industry, without directly cutting sick pay entitlements.
Previous negotiations broke down when the two sides failed to agree a system under which sick pay would be maintained at 100 percent of salary in return for cuts in holiday entitlements.

Talks in North Rhine-Westphalia were based on an entirely new approach under which low overall absenteeism in a company would be rewarded by higher end-of-year bonuses, while high sickness rates would mean lower bonuses.
But Kannegiesser said that while employer negiotators had originally thought such a model could offer them the cost savings they sought, they ultimately rejected it as unworkable.

Overall, metal and engineering employers are seeking a 1997 wage deal that would leave overall labour costs in the sector unchanged. Union leaders aim to secure agreements protecting jobs in the sector.
